# Training {#sec-sys-training}

A training run is a long, expensive, failure-prone distributed job. This
chapter explains how training infrastructure got the shape it has: why
parallelism is split the way it is, why checkpointing is non-negotiable,
and why scaling laws let you plan a run before you start it. By the end a
reader can explain why a training choice changes the result, not only that
it does.

## Problem

The model does not fit on one device, the data does not fit in memory, and
the hardware fails mid-run. The constraints are memory, interconnect
bandwidth, fault rate, and cost over days of occupancy.

## Design

Combined parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) to place a model that
does not fit on one device, a streaming input pipeline that does not starve
the accelerator, and asynchronous checkpoints that make a run resumable.

## Evolution

From single-device training, to data-parallel synchronous SGD, to the
tensor and pipeline parallelism of Megatron and GPipe, to ZeRO-style
sharding. Trace why each was forced by growing model size.

## Trade-offs

Each parallelism axis costs communication. Larger batches reduce noise but
raise the smallest useful step. Spot capacity cuts cost but raises the
preemption rate. Where the boundaries sit.

## In practice

Reproducibility and provenance, pinning data and code and config, gang
scheduling, detecting a silently diverging run, and resuming exactly across
a changing node count.

## Foundations

Why training works and why the dials matter. Stochastic gradient methods
and the variance of the gradient estimate, the batch-size to learning-rate
relationship, and scaling laws as a planning tool.

$$
L(N, D) = L_\infty + \left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N} + \left(\frac{D_c}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D}
$$
